headline: The plan does not fit the 8m window. 11 artifacts will not survive it. The order the plan is written in preserves as much as the recommended order does.

plan.name: MFG-DB-11 — privilege escalation, fixed maintenance window

asset.name: MFG-DB-11.plant.internal
asset.description: Database server for the plant execution system. The approved maintenance procedure requires the host to be shut down before the upgrade.
asset.notes: The maintenance window is fixed by the production schedule and cannot be extended without stopping the line.

vulnerability.title: Local privilege escalation in the database engine
vulnerability.summary: A flaw in the engine permits a local account to escalate to the engine service account. Exploitation reported in the wild.

tier.label: Critical — 3 day
tier.notes: The remediation tier allows three days. The operational window allows eight minutes. Those are two different constraints and only one of them is negotiable.

accepted_losses.what_is_lost: Live memory will not be acquired. The physical memory image, and with it any unbacked executable regions and resident key material, will not exist after the shutdown.
accepted_losses.why_necessary: The approved maintenance procedure begins with a shutdown at a fixed time set by the production schedule. A memory acquisition takes approximately forty-five minutes against an eight-minute window, and the line cannot be held.
accepted_losses.alternative_considered: A targeted dump of the database engine process was considered at roughly eight minutes. It was rejected because it would consume the entire window and leave no time for the upgrade itself.
accepted_losses.residual_risk: If the host was compromised through the escalation flaw, we will be unable to determine whether anything was executing that never touched disk. A disk-based investigation remains possible and the audit log is being preserved.

plan.notes: The plan does not fit the window and everyone involved knows it. What this analysis adds is the list of exactly what is being given up, and a record of who decided.

artifacts.name: Physical memory image
artifacts.description: A full image of the host RAM, including kernel structures, process address spaces and anything resident that never touched disk.

collection.label: Live acquisition to external storage
collection.observer_effect: The acquisition agent runs in the memory it is imaging, so the image includes the act of taking it and is not a consistent point-in-time snapshot.
collection.note: Scales with installed RAM and the write speed of the destination.

artifacts.answers: Was anything executing that never existed as a file? Fileless malware, injected code and in-memory credentials exist nowhere else.

artifacts.name: Target process memory
artifacts.description: The address space of one specific process — typically the vulnerable service — dumped without imaging the whole host.

collection.label: Per-process memory dump
collection.observer_effect: Dumping a running process may briefly suspend it, and the dump reflects the moment of collection rather than the moment of interest.
collection.note: The pragmatic substitute when a full memory image will not fit the window.

artifacts.answers: What was inside the vulnerable service at the time — deserialised payloads, request buffers, loaded webshell code?

artifacts.name: Unbacked executable memory
artifacts.description: Executable memory regions with no backing file on disk — the usual shape of process injection and reflectively loaded code.

collection.label: Region enumeration and targeted dump
collection.note: Depends on a live process list; loses meaning once processes have been restarted.

artifacts.answers: Is code running on this host that was never written to disk, and therefore leaves no file for anyone to find afterwards?

artifacts.name: Decrypted key material in memory
artifacts.description: Private keys, session keys and secrets that exist in plaintext only while the process holding them is running.

collection.label: Extracted from a memory image
collection.note: No independent estimate: in practice this is recovered from the memory image rather than collected separately, and the time is analysis time rather than acquisition time.

artifacts.answers: Which secrets were actually resident and therefore reachable by anything running on this host?
artifacts.notes: Recovery from an image is not guaranteed; some runtimes zero key buffers aggressively and some do not.

artifacts.name: Running process list
artifacts.description: Processes with command lines, parents, owning users and start times, as a point-in-time list.

collection.label: Process enumeration to file
collection.observer_effect: The collection tool appears in its own output.

artifacts.answers: What was actually running, under whose account, launched by what? The parent chain is usually the first thing an investigation asks for.

artifacts.name: Loaded modules
artifacts.description: Shared libraries, drivers and kernel modules loaded into running processes and into the kernel.
artifacts.answers: Was anything loaded into a legitimate process that did not belong there — a sideloaded library, an unsigned driver?

artifacts.name: Open handles and deleted-but-open files
artifacts.description: Open file and socket handles, including files that have been unlinked from the filesystem but are still held open by a process.

collection.label: Handle enumeration, with recovery of unlinked files
collection.note: An unlinked-but-open file is recoverable only while the holding process lives.

artifacts.answers: Is there a file the attacker deleted that is still recoverable because something still has it open? After the process ends, it is not.

artifacts.name: Service runtime state
artifacts.description: The running configuration, uptime, worker set and in-memory state of the affected service, as distinct from its configuration on disk.

collection.label: Service status and runtime configuration dump

artifacts.answers: Was the service running the configuration that is on disk, or something that was changed at runtime and never written down?

artifacts.name: Established network connections
artifacts.description: The socket table: established connections with remote addresses, ports and owning processes.
artifacts.answers: Where was this host talking to, right now, and which process owned the conversation? A closed connection leaves no local record of itself.

artifacts.name: Listening sockets
artifacts.description: Bound ports and the processes listening on them.
artifacts.answers: Was anything listening that should not have been — a backdoor port, an unexpected bind?

artifacts.name: ARP / neighbour cache
artifacts.description: Recently resolved layer-2 neighbours on the local segment.
artifacts.answers: Which hosts on the local segment did this machine actually talk to recently?

artifacts.name: DNS resolver cache
artifacts.description: Names this host resolved recently, with their remaining time to live.

collection.label: Resolver cache dump
collection.note: Entries expire on their own; the cache is a partial record even before anything touches it.

artifacts.answers: What names did this host look up? Often the only local trace of a command-and-control domain if egress logging is thin.
artifacts.notes: Cache contents are already lossy: TTL expiry removes entries with no record that they existed.

artifacts.name: Logged-on sessions
artifacts.description: Interactive and remote sessions currently established, with their origin.
artifacts.answers: Who is logged in right now, from where, and since when?

artifacts.name: Shared memory and tmpfs
artifacts.description: Shared memory segments and memory-backed filesystems, which look like files but do not survive a reboot.
artifacts.answers: Was anything staged somewhere that looks like disk but is not? Content here is frequently mistaken for something a disk image will capture.

artifacts.name: Temporary directory contents
artifacts.description: World-writable and per-user temporary paths, the usual staging ground.
artifacts.answers: What was staged and not yet cleaned up?
artifacts.notes: Some platforms clear temporary paths on boot and some do not; treat survival across a reboot as configuration-dependent.

artifacts.name: Swap and pagefile
artifacts.description: Paged-out memory on disk, which can retain fragments of process memory long after the process has gone.

collection.label: Copy of the swap device or pagefile
collection.note: Often locked while the host is running; may need to be taken from the disk image instead.

artifacts.answers: Is there a fragment of a process that has already exited? Sometimes the only remaining trace of a short-lived payload.
artifacts.notes: Some deployments run without swap, and encrypted swap is unreadable after a reboot even if the file survives.

artifacts.name: Crash dumps and core files
artifacts.description: Process cores and system crash dumps already written to disk.
artifacts.answers: Did the exploit crash something on the way in? A failed attempt often leaves a core file that a successful one does not.

artifacts.name: Staged tooling in writable paths
artifacts.description: Binaries, scripts and archives left in paths the service account can write to.
artifacts.answers: What did they bring with them, and what does it tell you about what they were doing?

artifacts.name: Full disk image
artifacts.description: A block-level image of the host storage.

collection.label: Block-level acquisition, or a cloud volume snapshot
collection.observer_effect: An image taken from a running host is internally inconsistent: different regions are captured at different moments.
collection.note: A cloud volume snapshot is dramatically faster than a physical acquisition and is the realistic path on a VM.

artifacts.answers: Everything on disk, as it was — the fallback for every question nobody thought to ask.

artifacts.name: Filesystem timestamps
artifacts.description: Created, modified, accessed and metadata-changed times across the filesystem, as a timeline.

collection.label: Filesystem metadata timeline
collection.observer_effect: Collection itself updates access times unless the filesystem is mounted read-only.

artifacts.answers: When did things change, and in what order? The backbone of almost every host timeline.
artifacts.notes: Timestamps are attacker-modifiable and are routinely modified. Treat the timeline as testimony, not as ground truth.

artifacts.name: Installed package and version state
artifacts.description: The installed package set, versions, and the package manager transaction history. On an appliance, the running firmware version and its upgrade history.
artifacts.answers: What was the vulnerable version, and what else was installed or changed recently? This is also the before-state the patch will overwrite.

artifacts.name: Persistence mechanisms
artifacts.description: Scheduled tasks, service units, autostart entries, cron, run keys and the other places something arranges to come back.
artifacts.answers: Will they come back after you fix this? The question a remediation that only patches does not answer.

artifacts.name: Service configuration on disk
artifacts.description: The configuration files the affected service reads at start-up.
artifacts.answers: Was the configuration tampered with? Also the record of what the service was before the change you are about to make.

artifacts.name: Local event and system logs
artifacts.description: Logs held on the host itself, before any forwarding.
artifacts.answers: What did the host record about itself — including anything that was never forwarded, and anything that was cleared.
artifacts.notes: Local logs are attacker-reachable. Their absence is itself a finding; their presence is not proof they are complete.

artifacts.name: Centralised log copies
artifacts.description: The same events as held off the host by the logging platform.

collection.label: Query and export from the log platform
collection.note: Held off the host, so nothing done to the host destroys them.

artifacts.answers: What survived off the host? Usually the only copy an attacker with host access could not edit.
artifacts.notes: Bounded by the platform retention window, which may be shorter than the incident.

artifacts.name: Endpoint telemetry
artifacts.description: Process, file and network telemetry recorded by the endpoint agent.
artifacts.answers: What did the agent see, including process ancestry for processes that have since exited?
artifacts.notes: Coverage depends on sensor configuration and on whether the agent was running throughout.

artifacts.name: Database audit log
artifacts.description: Statement and connection auditing recorded by the database engine.
artifacts.answers: What was read, and how much of it? The question the disclosure decision turns on.
artifacts.notes: Auditing is frequently configured to record connections but not statements, in which case the volume read is not recoverable from this source.

actions.name: Acquire physical memory
actions.description: Image host RAM to external storage. Recovers injected code and resident key material as a side effect, because both live in the image.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.notes: The single longest step in most plans, and the first to be cut when the clock is tight. That trade-off is the one worth arguing about in the open.

actions.name: Dump target process memory
actions.description: Dump the address space of the affected service only, recovering injected regions and resident secrets belonging to that process. The realistic substitute when a full memory image will not fit the window, and the only memory option on a container, which has no memory image of its own.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.notes: Covers the target process only. Injection into any other process on the host is not covered and will not be detected by this step.

actions.name: Snapshot running state
actions.description: Process list, loaded modules, open handles and service runtime configuration.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.notes: Cheap, fast, and the step most often skipped because it feels redundant next to a memory image. It is not: it is readable immediately.

actions.name: Snapshot network state
actions.description: Socket table, listeners, neighbour cache and resolver cache.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.name: Enumerate sessions and tickets
actions.description: Logged-on sessions, plus the cached Kerberos tickets where the platform has them. Applies everywhere something can be logged in; the ticket cache is host-only and is filtered out where it does not apply.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.name: Collect runtime and temporary paths
actions.description: Memory-backed paths, temporary directories, staged tooling and crash dumps.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.name: Collect host triage set
actions.description: Package state, persistence mechanisms, served-path contents, service configuration and a filesystem metadata timeline.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.notes: Includes the pre-patch package state, which the upgrade will overwrite. Skipping this step is how a team ends up unable to say which version was actually exposed.

actions.name: Acquire full disk image
actions.description: Block-level acquisition of host storage, including swap.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.notes: Rarely fits a short remediation window. On a cloud VM, take a volume snapshot instead.

actions.name: Export host logs
actions.description: Export the logs held on the host, before anything rotates or rebuilds it.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.name: Export off-host records
actions.description: Pull the centralised log copies and endpoint telemetry for the affected window.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.notes: These records are off the host, so nothing done to the host destroys them. They can usually wait — the reason to do them early is platform retention, not remediation.

actions.name: Export database audit log
actions.description: Export statement and connection auditing for the affected window.

default_effect.rationale: A capture reads. It does not remediate anything and destroys nothing.

actions.name: Restart affected service
actions.description: Stop and start the affected service. The most common remediation step, and the one most often assumed to be harmless.

effects.rationale: The process whose memory you wanted is replaced by a fresh one. Its address space is returned to the operating system.
The running configuration is rebuilt from disk. Anything set at runtime and never written down is gone.
Secrets held by the service exist only while it is running.
Code injected into the restarted service goes with it. Injection into any other process on the host is untouched, so this is a partial loss that the plan cannot narrow further.
A file the attacker unlinked but left open by this service becomes unrecoverable the moment the process ends.
Connections owned by the service are torn down. The rest of the socket table survives, so what you collect afterwards is a partial picture that looks like a complete one.
The service unbinds and rebinds. An unexpected extra listener may not come back.
Process identifiers and start times for the service change, which breaks the parent chain from before the restart.
Segments owned by the service may be released when it exits.
If the session store is held in the application process it is destroyed; if it is an external cache or table it is untouched. Which one this deployment uses is not recorded here.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.reference: Synthetic mapping. Derived from how service managers replace processes.
actions.notes: A restart is frequently treated as a non-event. It is the single cheapest way to destroy the memory of the process you are investigating.

actions.name: Reboot host
actions.description: Restart the operating system.

effects.rationale: Memory contents do not survive a reset. This is the clearest evidence-destroying relationship in the library.
Every process on the host is replaced. Nothing about the previous set survives in memory.
The network stack reinitialises. Sockets, caches and neighbour tables all start empty.
Sessions and cached tickets on the host do not survive the reset.
Memory-backed filesystems are memory. They look like disk and behave like RAM.
Whether the layer survives depends on whether the orchestrator restarts the existing container or schedules a new one. That is a property of your restart policy, not of the reboot.
Some platforms clear temporary paths at boot and some do not. Treat survival as configuration-dependent rather than assured.
The swap area is reinitialised or reused on boot. Where swap is encrypted with an ephemeral key, its contents become unreadable even though the file survives.
The log gains shutdown and boot records, and anything buffered but not yet flushed at shutdown is lost.
Boot activity updates access and modification times across system paths, adding noise to a timeline that has not yet been captured.
Stored state survives a reset. A reboot is not a rebuild.
Records already held off the host cannot be reached by anything done to the host.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.reference: Synthetic mapping. Derived from the definition of a power-cycle.

actions.name: Shut down host
actions.description: Power the host off, typically because a maintenance procedure requires it.

effects.rationale: Memory contents do not survive loss of power.
Nothing is running afterwards.
Nothing is connected afterwards.
Sessions on the host end with the host.
Memory-backed filesystems are memory.
Stored state survives a clean shutdown, and the disk can still be imaged offline.
Records already held off the host are unaffected.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.notes: A shutdown ends every opportunity that required a live host. Anything with `requires_live_host` that has not been collected by this point cannot be collected at all.

actions.name: Terminate process
actions.description: Kill a specific process — typically one identified as malicious.

effects.rationale: The address space is returned to the operating system when the process exits.
Regions belonging to the terminated process go with it.
Secrets held by the process are freed with its memory.
Any file the process held open after unlinking it is released, and at that moment it stops being recoverable.
The list changes. Children of the terminated process may be reparented or die with it.
Connections owned by the process close.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.notes: Terminating a suspicious process before dumping it is the most common way an investigation loses its primary artifact.

actions.name: Isolate host from network
actions.description: Apply network quarantine so the host can no longer reach anything but management.

effects.rationale: Established connections are torn down by the quarantine. The socket table afterwards records the isolation, not the incident.
Entries age out with nothing refreshing them.
If the host can no longer reach the logging platform, forwarding stops. Events after this point exist only on the host.
Whether the endpoint agent keeps its management channel under your quarantine policy is a property of that policy, which is not recorded here.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.notes: Isolation is usually filed under "safe". It is safe for the estate and destructive for network state — and it may quietly stop the off-host logging you were relying on.

actions.name: Replace binary
actions.description: Overwrite the vulnerable executable or library in place.

effects.rationale: The replaced file carries the replacement times. Whatever the original timestamps said is gone unless already recorded.
The on-disk state no longer matches what the package manager believes is installed.
An image taken after this point no longer contains the vulnerable binary, which is often the artifact the investigation needs to hash.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.name: Apply package upgrade
actions.description: Upgrade the vulnerable package through the platform package manager.

effects.rationale: The on-disk state of the vulnerable version is overwritten. This is the record of what you were actually exposed to, and the patch is what removes it — which is why it is captured before rather than after.
Every file the upgrade touches gets new times, over the top of the timeline you wanted.
Upgrades may replace, merge or back up configuration files. A tampered configuration can be quietly normalised.
An image taken afterwards is of the patched system, not the exposed one.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.notes: Modelled as the package operation alone. Most package managers also restart the service; where yours does, add the restart as its own step so its footprint is counted.

actions.name: Apply configuration change
actions.description: Change the service configuration — a mitigation, a hardening step, or disabling the vulnerable feature.

effects.rationale: The pre-change configuration is overwritten. If it had been tampered with, the tampering is what you have just deleted.
The configuration files carry new modification times.
The running configuration diverges from what it was when the incident occurred.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.name: Rotate credential
actions.description: Issue a new secret for the affected service account, key or certificate.

effects.rationale: Rotation is the point of the action, but it also ends your ability to observe what the old credential could still reach. Inventory the live tokens first or the blast radius becomes unknowable.
Sign-in history is a record of the past. Changing a secret does not edit it.
The directory audit trail is appended to, not rewritten.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.notes: Rotation does not destroy stored records. What it destroys is visibility: after it, nobody can enumerate what the compromised credential was still able to do.

actions.name: Terminate active sessions
actions.description: Force-close interactive and remote sessions on the affected asset or principal.

effects.rationale: The sessions are the thing being ended.
Connections carrying those sessions close.
Off-host records are unaffected.

default_effect.rationale: This action is bounded to the component named above. Everything else on the host, including all stored state, is outside what it touches.

actions.name: Rebuild host
actions.description: Reimage the host from a known-good build.

effects.rationale: Nothing about the old host survives.
Nothing about the old host survives.
Nothing about the old host survives.
Nothing about the old host survives.
Nothing about the old host survives.
Nothing about the old host survives.
The storage is overwritten by the new build.
Held on the storage being overwritten.
Records already held off the host are the only thing a rebuild cannot reach. After a rebuild they are the investigation.

default_effect.rationale: This action replaces the host. Anything held on it and not explicitly listed above should be assumed gone.

actions.name: Verify remediation
actions.description: Confirm the fix is in place and the service is healthy.

default_effect.rationale: Verification reads the system. It changes nothing in the evidence catalogue.

steps.name: Snapshot running state
steps.why_now: Running process list, Loaded modules, Open handles and deleted-but-open files and 1 other decay on their own — connections close, processes exit, caches expire — so this runs first regardless of what the plan does. "Shut down host" is the first step in this plan that reaches them; after it, this capture would collect nothing.

steps.name: Shut down host
steps.why_now: A remediation step. Physical memory image, Target process memory, Unbacked executable memory and 7 others stop existing here, which is why everything above it had to run first.

steps.name: Apply package upgrade
steps.why_now: A remediation step. Installed package and version state stops existing here, which is why everything above it had to run first.

steps.name: Verify remediation
steps.why_now: A remediation step. Nothing in the evidence catalogue is lost at this point.

steps.name: Export database audit log
steps.why_now: Nothing in this plan reaches Database audit log, so this capture is not racing anything. It is placed after remediation so it does not spend time on the clock before the fix. Platform retention, not this plan, is what bounds it.

gates.reason: "Shut down host" is the first step in this plan that reaches Running process list, Loaded modules, Open handles and deleted-but-open files and Service runtime state. Everything in this gate has to be collected before the step below it runs.

feasibility.explanation: 57m of work against a 8m window, which overruns by 49m. Preserving everything currently planned and meeting the stated deadline are not both possible. Something has to give, and choosing what is not a decision this tool makes.

conflicts.title: Preservation and the deadline are incompatible
conflicts.detail: 57m of preservation, remediation, verification and buffer against a 8m window: an overrun of 49m. Preserving everything currently planned and meeting the stated deadline are not both possible.
options: Reduce the collection scope: drop optional artifacts and keep the required ones.
Prioritise by volatility: keep the captures that cannot be repeated later and defer the ones that can.
Delay remediation with an approved exception, so the window moves rather than the evidence.
Change the collection method: a targeted process dump instead of a full memory image, a volume snapshot instead of a disk acquisition.
Accept the loss of specific named artifacts and record who decided that.

conflicts.title: 8 artifacts will not survive this plan, and nobody has signed for them
conflicts.detail: Target process memory, Established network connections, Listening sockets, ARP / neighbour cache and 4 others. Losing evidence during remediation is frequently the right call. Losing it without a record of who decided and why is the part that becomes a problem six months later, when somebody asks what was known at the time.
options: Record an accepted loss for each artifact, naming the decision owner and the residual risk.
Reorder so the captures precede the destructive steps.
Reduce the remediation to steps that do not destroy this evidence, if an equivalent mitigation exists.

conflicts.title: 5 required artifacts have no capture step in this plan
conflicts.detail: Physical memory image, Target process memory, Unbacked executable memory, Established network connections and 1 other are marked required, and the plan contains a step that reaches them. Nothing in the plan collects them first. What goes unanswered: Physical memory image — Was anything executing that never existed as a file? Fileless malware, injected code and in-memory credentials exist nowhere else. Target process memory — What was inside the vulnerable service at the time — deserialised payloads, request buffers, loaded webshell code? Unbacked executable memory — Is code running on this host that was never written to disk, and therefore leaves no file for anyone to find afterwards?
options: Add the corresponding capture steps before the steps that reach them.
Downgrade any artifact the investigation does not in fact need, so the plan stops claiming to require it.
Record each loss as a decision, with a named owner and the residual risk.

assumptions: Steps run one after another on a single worker. Two captures that could genuinely run in parallel are counted twice against the clock, so the total is conservative.
The evidence catalogue is scoped to database server. Artifacts that do not apply to this asset type are not offered and are not counted as lost.
Durations are order-of-magnitude figures from the catalogue, adjusted by any per-step override in this plan. They are not measurements of your environment.
Verification (0 min) and contingency buffer (5 min) are counted against the window as stated in the plan.
The remediation tier and the deadline are inputs. TOURNIQUET does not assess how urgent this vulnerability is and cannot tell you whether the tier is right.
limitations: TOURNIQUET plans an order. It does not acquire evidence, does not execute remediation, and has no connection to any system.

The action-to-evidence mappings are a synthetic library written for this tool. They describe how these platforms generally behave; they are not vendor statements and they are not tested against your build.
Confidence is declared per mapping and propagated. It is not derived from any corpus, and "high" means "follows from how the platform works", not "measured".

An artifact reported as retained is retained under the plan as analysed. Anything not in the plan — a colleague restarting the service, an autoscaler replacing the node — is outside what this can see.
Timestamps, package state and local logs are attacker-modifiable. Preserving them preserves what is there, which is not the same as preserving the truth.
The tool cannot tell you whether an investigation is warranted. It tells you what a given remediation would cost you if one turned out to be.
